variants.name: Play global HttpFilters chain
variants.implementation_notes: Play's filter API applies a global chain to every request: implement `Filter` (curried apply(nextFilter)(requestHeader)) or `EssentialFilter` when the body must be inspected, register the instances through HttpFilters or play.http.filters, and reject by returning a Future[Result] with 400 instead of invoking nextFilter. Filters replace an interceptor class hierarchy and are the framework's designated indiscriminate cross-cutting layer - Play explicitly contrasts them with action composition, which is route-specific. Filters run after the router, so path/body checks that must precede routing need an HttpRequestHandler or an EssentialFilter.
pitfalls: Filters run after routing, so they cannot reject based on the raw path/body before the router matched; use an EssentialFilter or request handler when that matters.
A Filter returning a failed Future surfaces as a server error rather than a validation rejection; model rejection as a Result and reserve exceptions for faults.
The implicit ExecutionContext/Materializer must be available; blocking work inside the filter should be avoided or shifted to a dedicated dispatcher.

variants.name: http4s functional middleware (Kleisli)
variants.implementation_notes: In http4s middleware is just a function taking one service and returning another (a Kleisli), so the validation layer is ordinary function composition: the middleware may inspect the Request, short-circuit by returning a response without calling the inner service, and compose with other middleware before routes are mounted (`validate(routes).orNotFound`). There is no class hierarchy, registry or implicit ordering - composition order is the chain order - which makes the layer trivially testable without a server, provided it is applied once at the single app entry point.
pitfalls: Because the chain is composition, nothing forces every route to be mounted through the middleware; compose once at the single entry point and test coverage explicitly.
The effect type F must stay consistent (IO vs OptionT wrapping) - mixing them changes the middleware's type and silently drops routes instead of failing to compile.
Per-request effects run inside F; validators must be pure or resource-safe, and blocking work needs a dedicated blocking pool.
